title: CELPIP Reading Practice Test 29
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer the questions. You may scroll back within each part.

emails.subject: Contamination charge, 14 Aldermoor Court — flats, shared bins
emails.body:
Dear Waste Services,

I have received a $60 contamination charge for the recycling bin at 14 Aldermoor Court, addressed to me personally.

I live in a block of nine flats. The recycling bin is a shared communal bin in a locked yard used by all nine households. I do not know who put the wrong material in it and neither, I assume, do you.

I am not writing to say it was not me, although it was not. I am writing about how the charge was allocated. My flat is number 1. I would like to know whether the charge was issued to me because the evidence points to me, or because my flat number sorts first in your system and the bin has one address attached to it.

If it is the first, I would like to see what the evidence is. If it is the second, then nine households share a bin and one household receives the bill, which is not a system that can produce the behaviour change the charge exists to create — the eight people who cannot be charged have no reason to change, and the one who can be charged cannot control what they do.

I would also like to know what I am supposed to do differently. I sort my own recycling correctly. I have no key to the yard other than for my own use and no authority over my neighbours.

Sincerely,
Lucienne Fournier-Doyle

emails.subject: RE: Contamination charge, 14 Aldermoor Court — flats, shared bins
emails.body:
Dear Ms Fournier-Doyle,

It is the second, and the charge is cancelled.

Our system attaches communal bins to the lowest flat number at the address. That is not a policy anyone adopted; it is what the database does when a bin has one address field and a building has nine households. You are the ninth resident to receive a charge under this arrangement this year, and you are the first to ask how it was allocated. The other eight paid.

I am refunding all eight. I would not have found them without your email, and I would rather tell you that than let you assume we ran a check.

Your second point is the one I have taken to the service review. You are right that a charge that cannot reach the person responsible and cannot be avoided by the person charged does not change behaviour; it just collects money from whoever the database names. I do not have authority to suspend the scheme for communal bins and I have recommended it, which is not the same thing and I will not pretend otherwise.

On what you can do differently: nothing, and I am not going to invent something. The realistic options are a bin store with individual containers, which is a landlord decision and a capital cost, or clearer signage in the yard, which we can supply free within two weeks if the managing agent asks. I have written to them. I have not had a reply and I cannot compel one.

Regards,
Ogechi Balogun
Waste Services Manager

passages.title: Harrowfield Recycling Centre & Collections — Winter Arrangements
passages.intro: Winter arrangements run December 1 to February 28. The Recycling Centre requires a free vehicle permit for vans and trailers, applied for online at least 3 working days ahead; cars need no permit. Bulky item collections must be booked and are charged per item. Garden waste collections are suspended for winter. Where a collection day falls on a public holiday, it moves to the following Saturday.

passages.title: Why Recycling Rates Stopped Rising
passages.content:
Recycling rates in many places climbed steeply for a decade and then flattened, and the plateau is usually attributed to public complacency. The evidence points somewhere less convenient: the easy material has already been captured, and what remains is harder for reasons that have little to do with willingness.

The early gains came from a small number of high-volume, easily separated materials — paper, card, glass, metal cans. These are dense, familiar and clearly identifiable, and capturing them produced a large percentage rise for modest effort. What is left in the residual bin is dominated by mixed materials, small items and things that are technically recyclable in a facility the local authority does not have. A resident sorting these correctly requires knowledge that changes by material, by manufacturer and by council area.

Inconsistency between areas is a documented and underrated barrier. Where neighbouring authorities accept different plastics, residents who move, or who compare notes, learn that the rules are local rather than physical — and once a rule is understood as arbitrary, compliance drops even where the rule is correct. National standardisation is dull, unpopular with authorities that have already invested in one system, and among the better-evidenced interventions available.

Contamination behaves in a way that surprises people. A small proportion of wrong material can render a whole load unrecyclable, so the marginal cost of one hopeful item in the wrong bin is far higher than its volume implies. Campaigns encouraging people to recycle more, without also clarifying what not to include, have in several documented cases raised collection volumes and lowered the amount actually recycled. Enthusiasm without specificity is measurably counterproductive.

The final constraint is that household behaviour is not where most of the material is. Packaging decisions made by manufacturers determine what a household can possibly do, and a container designed with mixed layers cannot be recycled by any sorting effort at the kerbside. Rates are therefore partly a measure of what industry has chosen to produce, presented as a measure of what residents have chosen to do.

The implication is that further gains depend less on persuading households and more on standardising rules, funding facilities for harder materials, and constraining what is put on shelves in the first place.

passages.title: Should Drinks Containers Carry a Refundable Deposit?

viewpoints.name: Minister Ottilie Ferrandes
viewpoints.text: We are introducing a deposit scheme and the evidence for return rates is strong, so I will spend my space on the objection I find hardest. Deposit schemes move material out of kerbside collection, and kerbside is funded partly by the value of exactly that material — cans and bottles are the profitable part of the load. So a successful scheme improves one number and worsens council recycling finances at the same time. That is real, it is not a reason not to do it, and it needs funding alongside rather than being discovered afterwards.

viewpoints.name: Marek Zielinski, small shop owner
viewpoints.text: I will host a return point and I am not opposed. My difficulty is space and time: a machine occupies floor area I sell from, and manual returns mean my one staff member counts bottles while a queue forms. The handling fee is calculated on volume returned, which suits a supermarket and does not suit me, because my costs are mostly fixed rather than per-container. Pay a floor amount to small retailers and the network gets the density it needs. Pay per unit only and you will get return points in supermarkets and nowhere else.

viewpoints.name: Dr Ingrid Halvorsen, waste systems researcher
viewpoints.text: Return rates under deposit schemes are consistently high and that finding is not seriously contested. What is contested, and frequently overstated, is the claim that deposits reduce total litter. They reduce container litter, which is visible and measurable; the effect on overall litter volume is smaller and sometimes absent, because other items are unaffected. I support the policy for material recovery, which is where the evidence is. I would stop selling it as a litter policy, because when litter does not visibly fall, that is what people will remember.

viewpoints.name: Kenneth Ofori-Boateng, kerbside collection crew
viewpoints.text: Everyone talks about where the bottles go and nobody asks what happens to my round. If the profitable material leaves the blue bin, the round takes the same time, uses the same fuel and returns less value — so the pressure lands on frequency, and reduced frequency is what residents will actually notice about this policy. I am not arguing against deposits. I am saying the people designing this should say out loud that collections may go fortnightly, rather than let that arrive later looking like an unrelated cut.
